title: Jude

stories.title: 📜 Jude
summaryBullets: Jude, a servant of Jesus Christ and a brother of James, To those who are called, loved by God the Father, and kept in Jesus Christ: (1:1).
Mercy, peace, and love be multiplied to you. (1:2).

Beloved, although I made every effort to write to you about the salvation we share, I felt it necessary to write and urge you to contend earnestly for the faith entrusted once for all to the saints. (1:3).

For certain men have crept in among you unnoticed — ungodly ones who were designated long ago for condemnation. They turn the grace of our God into a license for immorality, and they deny our only Master and Lord, Jesus Christ. (1:4).
Although you are fully aware of this, I want to remind you that after Jesus had delivered His people out of the land of Egypt, He destroyed those who did not believe. (1:5).
And the angels who did not stay within their own domain but abandoned their proper dwelling— these He has kept in eternal chains under darkness, bound for judgment on that great day. (1:6).

In like manner, Sodom and Gomorrah and the cities around them, who indulged in sexual immorality and pursued strange flesh, are on display as an example of those who sustain the punishment of eternal fire. (1:7).
Yet in the same way these dreamers defile their bodies, reject authority, and slander glorious beings. (1:8).
But even the archangel Michael, when he disputed with the devil over the body of Moses, did not presume to bring a slanderous charge against him, but said, “The Lord rebuke you!” (1:9).
These men, however, slander what they do not understand, and like irrational animals, they will be destroyed by the things they do instinctively. (1:10).
Woe to them! They have traveled the path of Cain; they have rushed for profit into the error of Balaam; they have perished in Korah’s rebellion. (1:11).

These men are hidden reefs in your love feasts, shamelessly feasting with you but shepherding only themselves. They are clouds without water, carried along by the wind; fruitless trees in autumn, twice dead after being uprooted. (1:12).
They are wild waves of the sea, foaming up their own shame; wandering stars, for whom blackest darkness has been reserved forever. (1:13).
Enoch, the seventh from Adam, also prophesied about them: “Behold, the Lord is coming with myriads of His holy ones (1:14).
to execute judgment on everyone, and to convict all the ungodly of every ungodly act of wickedness and every harsh word spoken against Him by ungodly sinners.” (1:15).
These men are discontented grumblers, following after their own lusts; their mouths spew arrogance; they flatter others for their own advantage. (1:16).
But you, beloved, remember what was foretold by the apostles of our Lord Jesus Christ (1:17).
when they said to you, “In the last times there will be scoffers who will follow after their own ungodly desires.” (1:18).
These are the ones who cause divisions, who are worldly and devoid of the Spirit. (1:19).
But you, beloved, by building yourselves up in your most holy faith and praying in the Holy Spirit, (1:20).
keep yourselves in the love of God as you await the mercy of our Lord Jesus Christ to bring you eternal life. (1:21).
And indeed, have mercy on those who doubt; (1:22).
save others by snatching them from the fire; and to still others show mercy tempered with fear, hating even the clothing stained by the flesh. (1:23).
Now to Him who is able to keep you from stumbling and to present you unblemished in His glorious presence, with great joy — (1:24).
to the only God our Savior be glory, majesty, dominion, and authority through Jesus Christ our Lord before all time, and now, and for all eternity. Amen. (1:25).

translationNotes.note: Military-style verb meaning to struggle or fight earnestly for the faith entrusted to God’s people.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: רָשָׁע (rāšāʿ), Greek: ἀσεβεῖς (asebeîs, NT), Aramaic: רשיעיא (rešīʿayyā)
translationNotes.note: Describes those who live without reverence for God, violating his covenant and moral order.

stories.keyTakeaway: Jude exhorts believers to contend for the faith against ungodly intruders who pervert grace and deny Christ.

intro:
Jude was written by Jude, the half-brother of Jesus and brother of James (Jude 1: "Jude, a servant of Jesus Christ and brother of James"). Jude was a son of Mary and Joseph and one of Jesus' four named brothers (James, Joseph or Joses, Simon, and Judas/Jude per Matthew 13:55 and Mark 6:3), plus unnamed sisters. Like his brother James, Jude did not believe in Jesus during Jesus' earthly ministry (John 7:5: "Even his brothers did not believe in him") but became a follower after the resurrection appearances. 1 Corinthians 9:5 mentions that "the brothers of the Lord" were married and traveled with their wives in Christian missionary work. Jude self-identifies in this letter as "brother of James" rather than as "brother of Jesus" out of humility (calling himself "a servant of Jesus Christ" instead), and by referencing his more famous brother James (the leader of the Jerusalem church and author of the Letter of James) he distinguishes himself from the other men named Jude/Judas in the early Christian community. The author of this letter must be carefully distinguished from the other men named Judas in the New Testament: he is NOT Judas Iscariot the betrayer of Jesus; he is NOT Judas son of James, the apostle (Luke 6:16; Acts 1:13; John 14:22), who was also called Thaddaeus (Matthew 10:3); he is NOT Judas Barsabbas, the Jerusalem prophet sent to Antioch with Silas (Acts 15:22, 27, 32); he is NOT Judas of Galilee, the failed messianic claimant mentioned by Gamaliel (Acts 5:37). Jude is specifically the half-brother of Jesus and the full brother of James the half-brother of Jesus. The English form "Jude" (rather than "Judas") is used in most modern translations specifically to distinguish him from Judas Iscariot; both names translate the same Greek Ioudas, which is itself the Greek form of the Hebrew Yehudah ("Judah," "praise"), the name of one of the twelve patriarchs (Genesis 29:35).

The letter was composed sometime between AD 65 and AD 80, with the lower end of that range being most likely if Jude wrote before 2 Peter (or alternatively if Jude wrote first and 2 Peter drew on him); the two letters share substantial content in their denunciation of false teachers (compare 2 Peter 2 with Jude 4-19). The place of composition is unknown but probably somewhere in Palestine or the broader eastern Mediterranean where Jesus' family had settled. The Roman emperor was Nero (AD 54-68), Galba (AD 68-69), Otho (AD 69), Vitellius (AD 69), Vespasian (AD 69-79), or Titus (AD 79-81), depending on the precise date. According to early Christian tradition preserved by Hegesippus (recorded by Eusebius in Ecclesiastical History 3.20), two of Jude's grandsons were brought before the emperor Domitian (AD 81-96), who was investigating surviving descendants of King David as potential messianic threats to his rule; the grandsons were peasant farmers who showed their work-hardened hands and explained that the kingdom they awaited was heavenly rather than earthly, and Domitian released them as harmless. Tradition variously holds that Jude himself ministered in Mesopotamia, Persia, Armenia, and Edessa, and that he was martyred (some accounts by axe or club, in Beirut or Persia or Mesopotamia), though no consistent early account survives. The audience of the letter is general ("to those who are called, beloved in God the Father and kept for Jesus Christ," Jude 1) rather than a single congregation or individual; Jude wrote to address an urgent crisis affecting churches generally.

Jude is the sixty-fifth book of the Christian Bible, the twenty-sixth book of the New Testament, and the seventh and last of the General Epistles (immediately before Revelation). At twenty-five verses (one chapter), Jude is one of the shorter books of the New Testament. The earliest surviving manuscript is Papyrus 72 (P72, the Bodmer Papyrus, c. AD 250-300), the same codex that preserves 1 Peter and 2 Peter; other early witnesses include Codex Sinaiticus and Codex Vaticanus (both 4th century AD). Jude is notable in the New Testament for being the only book that directly quotes the apocryphal book of 1 Enoch as prophecy: Jude 14-15 ("It was also about these that Enoch, the seventh from Adam, prophesied, saying, 'Behold, the Lord comes with ten thousands of his holy ones, to execute judgment on all and to convict all the ungodly of all their deeds of ungodliness that they have committed in such an ungodly way, and of all the harsh things that ungodly sinners have spoken against him'") is a direct quotation of 1 Enoch 1:9 (the apocalyptic Jewish text traditionally attributed to Enoch the seventh from Adam, present in the Ethiopian Orthodox canon and quoted as authoritative by Jude). Jude also references the dispute between the archangel Michael and the devil over the body of Moses (Jude 9), which derives from the Jewish work the Assumption of Moses (or possibly the Testament of Moses), an account not preserved in the canonical Old Testament. Jude originally intended to write a general letter "about our common salvation" (Jude 3) but felt compelled to redirect to "contend for the faith that was once for all delivered to the saints" because of false teachers who had "crept in unnoticed... ungodly people, who pervert the grace of our God into sensuality and deny our only Master and Lord, Jesus Christ" (Jude 4). The letter closes with one of the most stirring benedictions in the New Testament (Jude 24-25): "Now to him who is able to keep you from stumbling and to present you blameless before the presence of his glory with great joy, to the only God, our Savior, through Jesus Christ our Lord, be glory, majesty, dominion, and authority, before all time and now and forever. Amen."
